transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-03-04 15:30 UTC | Duration: 52 minutes | Platform: Zoom | Recording: yes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Elena Ruiz (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Haven CTO), Aisha Khan (Haven Head of MLOps), Daniel Park (Haven Infra), Lina Gomez (Haven PM)

Summary: Quick discovery focused on unit economics for hosted vs dedicated vs private. Customer is cost-sensitive, wants predictable per-token unit costs and clear levers (batching, caching, quantization) to hit budget. They asked about security (SOC2/KMS) and benchmarking options.

Topics: cost per token, batching/caching levers, dedicated reservation economics, latency vs cost tradeoffs, security/compliance, benchmark next steps

--- Transcript ---
00:00 Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samir, AE at Redwood, and with me is Elena, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
00:07 Marcus: Good, thanks. Lots to cover, we want to understand the cost picture — hosted versus dedicated versus private — and what levers we actually have to push down unit cost.
00:14 Elena: Totally. We'll try to walk through the math and then talk about practical levers like batching, prefix caching, and quantization. Quick q: what are your current workloads?
00:22 Aisha: We're running a mix — about 500k tokens/day of generation for internal assistants and reranking for search. Most of it is latency-sensitive, 200ms p50 target for the assistant. We're also experimenting with embeddings for fresh data.
00:35 Daniel: And infra-wise we're on GCP mostly, some on-prem for sensitive things. Security is a hard req — SOC2, SAML SSO, KMS for key management.
00:42 Samir: Great, that maps to a lot of other customers. On hosted, we price per-token with tiers — we can send the spreadsheet — dedicated is reserved capacity which changes the unit economics because you amortize GPU hours.
00:53 Marcus: Can you give a quick example? Like if we do 500k tokens/day what's the difference?
00:59 Elena: Sure, rough back-of-envelope: hosted per-token for a medium model is X cents per 1k tokens — (transcription: "ex cents" unclear) — for dedicated, if you reserve a set of GPUs, the effective per-token can drop by 30-60% depending on utilization and batching. Key is utilization: if you hit 60-80% utilization on dedicated, costs fall dramatically.
01:20 Aisha: What about latency? If we batch aggressively to save cost, won't p50 blow up?
01:25 Elena: Right, that's the tradeoff. Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching and latency-aware routing so you can set latency SLOs and the system will avoid batching that violates SLOs. We also do prefix/KV caching for repeated prompts which can reduce token compute by 20-40% in many assistant workflows.
01:42 Marcus: What's prefix caching again?
01:45 Elena: It's where the KV cache for the model stores repeated prefixes so subsequent requests avoid re-computing early layers. So if your prompts have a stable system prompt, you only compute the delta tokens.
01:55 Marcus: Hmm, sounds promising. How easy is it to measure this impact?
01:58 Elena: We can run a benchmark with your real prompt set and measure effective token reduction and latency. We'll drop logs and token-level cost breakdowns.
02:06 Lina: On the hosted price you said X cents, is that public?
02:09 Samir: I'll send the exact tiered spreadsheet after the call — apologies the number in the call is fuzzy — but hosted is straightforward usage-based billing. The dedicated pricing has a monthly reservation component.
02:18 Daniel: For dedicated, if we underutilize do we still pay the reservation?
02:22 Samir: Yes the reserved commit is billed regardless, so you need to plan utilization. We help with autoscale and burst policies so you can reduce cold capacity cost, but the reservation is the economic lever.
02:32 Marcus: What about private / on-prem? It's more expensive but we might need it for compliance. How does the unit economics there look?
02:37 Elena: Private tends to be higher unit cost because you're buying the infra + maintenance. The upside is control over data residency and no egress. Many customers start on hosted, then move to dedicated as they scale, and some edge cases move to private. We can model both.
02:50 Aisha: Can you talk about quantization? We hear 4-bit and QAT options. What's the real savings?
02:54 Elena: Quantization can reduce GPU memory footprint and increase throughput. With 4-bit quantization you might see 1.5x-2x throughput improvement depending on hardware and model architecture; cost improvement varies. We provide recommended quantization profiles per model and workload; we also validate quality degradation on your eval set.
03:11 Marcus: And how do fallbacks work? If quality drops after quant we need quick rollback.
03:16 Elena: We support pinning model versions and automatic rollback policies. You can run canaries and A/B tests through the console.
03:22 Marcus: Security checklist — SOC2, SAML, audit logs, KMS. Do you have customer-managed KMS?
03:27 Samir: Yes, supported for Dedicated and Private. Hosted can integrate with customer-managed KMS depending on the contract; SOC 2 and SSO are standard. We'll share the security pack.
03:36 Daniel: For the benchmark run, what instrumentation do you collect?
03:39 Elena: Token-level latency, per-route cost, KV cache hits, batch sizes, GPU utilization, and tail latencies. We'll give a dashboard and raw CSVs.
03:49 Marcus: Ok, budget wise our finance asked for a 6-figure annual cap ceiling for this initiative. We need a predictable APU (per-prompt unit) to justify.
03:58 Samir: Understood. For reserved Dedicated we can show a committed spend profile that maps to a lower APU. Hosted is more variable but easier to start. We typically model three scenarios: low, expected, and high usage and show per-token effective cost.
04:12 Aisha: Do you have examples from other customers with similar token counts?
04:15 Samir: Yes — I can anonymize two customers. One at ~1M tokens/day moved to dedicated and cut effective token cost by ~45% after optimizing batching and enabling prefix cache. Another stayed hosted and used caching + smaller model variants for non-critical routes to keep cost steady.
04:31 Marcus: For the assistant we need p50 ~200ms and p99 under 800ms. Can dedicated hit that while still being cost-effective?
04:39 Elena: Yes, usually. Dedicated with local GPUs and low latency routing is best for tight SLOs. Hosted has regions optimized for low latency too, but if you need guaranteed throughput it's easier with reserved capacity.
04:50 Lina: If we go dedicated, what's the procurement lead time for reserved capacity?
04:53 Samir: Typically 2–4 weeks for provisioning once terms are agreed; private/on-prem is longer.
04:58 Marcus: A few follow-ups: 1) Can you send a hosted vs dedicated cost spreadsheet + assumptions? 2) Can we run a 1-week benchmark with our prompts? 3) Security docs.
05:09 Samir: Yep — we'll do all three. Elena will run the bench.
05:13 Elena: One note on batching levers: two types — client-side microbatching and server-side continuous batching. Client-side gives you control over request windows; server-side is better when you have lots of small requests. Hybrid approach often wins.
05:26 Aisha: Are there any hidden costs? Data egress, storage of cache, logs?
05:30 Samir: We'll call out egress to other clouds; storage for logs is an add-on if you need longer retention. We try to make the model clear in the spreadsheet.
05:37 Daniel: If we want to test quant profiles, do you support QAT?
05:40 Elena: We support evaluation with quantized runtimes and can recommend QAT if needed; full QAT requires model access and is rarer for third-party models but possible for customers that want to re-train.
05:50 Marcus: Who from Redwood will be our contact?
05:52 Samir: I'll own commercial and coordination; Elena will run the technical bench.
05:56 Lina: Great. Any objections from finance if we start on hosted and then commit to dedicated?
06:01 Samir: Not usually — many customers start hosted, validate, then switch. We can structure a pilot to convert credits to reservation to reduce friction.
06:10 Marcus: Let's talk timeline — we want a benchmark next week and a procurement decision in three weeks if numbers look good.
06:16 Samir: Sounds reasonable. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the benchmark plan.
06:20 (cross-talk)
06:25 Elena: Quick technical note — for embedding-heavy routes, caching is less effective but batching and smaller model variants help a lot.
06:34 Marcus: Any mentions of competitor pricing?
06:36 Samir: They asked about Anthropic and OpenAI; we discussed differences in fairness and throughput. We'll include competitive notes.
06:44 Aisha: Thanks — main risks we see are unpredictable spikes and quant quality regression.
06:49 Elena: For spikes we recommend a hybrid reserved + burst model; for quality we'll tie regressions to eval suites and create rollback policies.
06:58 Samir: Ok wrapping up — recap of next steps then action items.
07:02 Samir: Recap: Samir send pricing spreadsheet and hosted vs dedicated models; Elena run bench with sample prompts; Marcus provide prompts and SLOs; security pack to be shared.
07:12 Marcus: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
07:15 Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard words, some numbers redacted in audio (X cents) — see spreadsheet for exact rates.

References mentioned: security pack (link to be sent), cost model spreadsheet (will be attached), benchmark dashboard (Redwood console link after run)
